name: Olaudah Equiano
title: Olaudah Equiano: his own voice against the trade in enslaved people
description: An autobiography that linked the memory of slavery, Christian faith, and the call to end the Atlantic slave trade.

sections.heading: Telling a life in his own voice
paragraphs: In 1789 Olaudah Equiano published his autobiography in London, known as The Interesting Narrative of the Life of Olaudah Equiano. He had also been called Gustavus Vassa. He had lived in slavery and gained his freedom; by writing, he spoke up in a society where the continuation of the Atlantic slave trade was being debated.

His account brings together experiences of seafaring, violence, learning, and religious searching. His Christian conversion holds an important place in the way he interprets his life. It is an autobiography with a public purpose: it lets us hear his voice and, at the same time, requires us to distinguish personal testimony from independent verification of each episode.

sections.heading: A memoir addressed to its readers
paragraphs: Equiano addressed his book to readers able to influence the debate over abolition. The 1789 dedication asks for compassion for those who suffered under the slave trade and connects that request with responsibility before God. Writing was thus a form of action, as well as an exercise of memory.

His part in the abolitionist movement reminds us that Black people were not simply the recipients of campaigns organized by others. They acted, wrote, and demanded change. The British Parliament includes Equiano among the figures of London’s Black community who contributed to that struggle.

reflection: Proverbs 31:8–9 calls us to “open your mouth for those with no voice” and to “judge righteously.” That command also requires us to listen to those who are speaking and have been ignored. Equiano’s story invites us to recognize the value of a person’s own voice against those who presume to decide for others.

Reading a painful testimony calls for respect and attention to its context. A Christian community can examine how it treats people who are exploited, which stories it listens to, and which practices it tolerates. Trust in Christ does not justify domination over another human being, nor does it allow us to use their suffering as a mere illustration.
review_note: We avoid stating a birthplace because of the debate among historians. His personal experiences are attributed to his autobiographical account. Original wording, with no passages reproduced.
